# ECON 0100 | Demo E

Demos are similar to Checkpoints, often taken directly from past semesters. Work through the problems and check your work against mine. Practice answering clearly and completely. Grab a classmate, find a study room, and work together on a whiteboard.

## The Duel of Diagon Alley’s Dwindling Dealers

Spell books had long been sold by many shops on Diagon Alley, with the number of sellers staying constant in the last 200 years.

<!-- Editor. The title and the first sentence are yours (23F MiniExam E, last year's Demo E). Every other sentence and every answer table is my proposal, marked or noted under its heading. The story runs many dealers (E1, E2), then Petunia alone (E3), then Petunia against Vernon (E4). E3.1 and E4.1 are set on Diagon Alley and E3.2 and E4.2 in Hogsmeade, so no question hands over another's answer. -->

### E2.1 | The Competitive Firm

### E2.2 | Entry, Exit & the Long Run

{++Anyone can open a spell book shop.++} The shops have identical marginal cost curves, $MC = 20 + 10q$, a price per book of $P = 40$, and the demand $D: P = 190 - Q$.

{++Each shop’s average total cost is lowest at 2 books a day, where it is 40 coins. Then the Ministry puts a tax of 10 coins on every spell book sold, which raises every shop’s marginal cost and average total cost by 10 coins at every quantity.++}

::: {.table style=plain inset=3pt columns="1fr auto"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Shops Before the Tax: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| At a Price of 40, Each Shop Makes a: | $\square$ profit $\quad\square$ loss |
| So Shops: | $\square$ enter $\quad\square$ exit |
| And the Price: | $\square$ rises $\quad\square$ falls |
| Long-Run Price With the Tax: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Each Shop’s Long-Run Quantity: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Long-Run Market Quantity: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Shops in the Long Run: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |

:::

### E3.1 | Monopoly Price & Quantity

{++Diagon Alley’s demand is $P = 190 - Q$, so the marginal revenue of Petunia’s Pages is $MR = 190 - 2Q$. Its marginal cost is $MC = 10 + 2Q$. The table shows its average total cost. Mark the quantity and the price on the graph, and shade the profit.++}

| **ATC** | 88 | 86 | 87 | 94 |

### E3.2 | Market Power & Deadweight Loss

{++Petunia’s Pages is also the only seller of spell books in Hogsmeade, a bigger market with demand $P = 250 - Q$. Its marginal cost there is the same, $MC = 10 + 2Q$. In Hogsmeade it sells 60 books a day at 190 coins each.++}

<!-- Editor. The form is the drafted stem E3.2_ferry-constant-cost with a rising marginal cost. The seller's price and quantity are given, so a slip in E3.1 costs nothing here. -->

::: {.table style=plain inset=3pt columns="1fr auto"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Efficient Quantity of Books: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Price at the Efficient Quantity: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Marginal Cost of the Last Book Petunia’s Pages Sells: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Deadweight Loss: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Compared With the Efficient Outcome, the Price Is: | $\square$ higher $\quad\square$ lower $\quad$ by \_\_\_\_\_\_ coins |
| Compared With the Efficient Outcome, the Quantity Is: | $\square$ higher $\quad\square$ lower $\quad$ by \_\_\_\_\_\_ books |

:::

### E4.1 | Best Responses in a Duopoly

{++Petunia’s brother Vernon opens **Vernon’s Volumes** on Diagon Alley with an identical bindery. The price is now $P = 190 - (q_P + q_V)$, so Petunia’s Pages has $MR_P = 190 - 2q_P - q_V$, and $MC_P = 10 + 2q_P$.++}

<!-- Editor. The marginal revenues are your 23F equations. The matrix is the high and low output bullet of E4.1, in Demo D's layout: Low is 30 books, the quantity that would give the two the most profit together, and High is 36. -->

::::: {.columns gutter=1.5em}

:::: column

::: {.table style=plain inset=3pt columns="1fr auto"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| If Vernon Sells 20, Petunia Sells: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Petunia’s Best Response: | $q_P =$ \_\_\_\_\_\_ $-$ \_\_\_\_\_\_ $q_V$ |

:::

### E4.2 | Duopoly Equilibrium

{++Vernon’s Volumes opens in Hogsmeade too, where the price is now $P = 250 - (q_P + q_V)$. When Petunia’s Pages was Hogsmeade’s only seller it sold 60 books at 190 coins. The two sellers are identical, and their best responses are $q_P = 60 - \tfrac{1}{4} q_V$ and $q_V = 60 - \tfrac{1}{4} q_P$.++}

<!-- Editor. The rows follow Exercise E4's Q2 and Q3: the best responses and the average total cost are given, and the last rows are Q3's efficiency check. -->

::: {.table style=plain inset=3pt columns="1fr auto"}

|   |   |
| :--- | :--- |
| Each Seller’s Nash Equilibrium Quantity: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Market Quantity: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Price: | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Total Profit of the Two Sellers (*each one’s ATC is 88*): | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| Compared With One Seller, the Price Is: | $\square$ higher $\quad\square$ lower $\quad$ by \_\_\_\_\_\_ coins |
| Compared With One Seller, the Market Quantity Is: | $\square$ higher $\quad\square$ lower $\quad$ by \_\_\_\_\_\_ books |
| Each Seller’s Marginal Cost at Its Quantity ($MC = 10 + 2q$): | \_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| The Duopoly Price Is: | $\square$ above $\quad\square$ equal to $\quad\square$ below marginal cost |
| So the Duopoly Outcome Is: | $\square$ efficient $\quad\square$ not efficient |

:::
